t.6.25.1: Then Saramā gladdened her, who was stricken with anguish and bewildered by those words, as the sky gladdens the earth with water.
t.6.25.2: Then her friend, wishing to do what was good for her companion, knowing the right moment and accustomed to speak with a smile, spoke these words at the proper time.
t.6.25.3: O dark-eyed lady, I would be able to go and convey your message and your well-being to Rāma, and then return unseen.
t.6.25.4: For when I stride through the unsupported sky, neither the wind nor even Garuḍa is able to follow my course.
t.6.25.5: To Saramā, who was speaking thus, Sītā replied sweetly, in a gentle voice still overcome by her former grief.
t.6.25.6: You are able to go to the sky or even to Rasātala. I understand what you ought to do and ought not to do on my behalf.
t.6.25.7: If you wish to do what is dear to me, and if your resolve is firm, then go to him, for I wish to know what Rāvaṇa is doing.
t.6.25.8: For that cruel Rāvaṇa, whose strength lies in illusion, who makes his enemies wail, that wicked-souled one bewilders me like vāruṇī wine the moment it is drunk.
t.6.25.9: He has me constantly threatened and repeatedly reviled by the most dreadful rākṣasīs who guard me day after day.
t.6.25.10: I am agitated and fearful, and my mind is not at ease; and, agitated by that fear, I have gone to the aśoka grove.
t.6.25.11: If there is indeed any talk of his, or whatever may have been decided, report all of that to me; that would be the greatest favor to me.
t.6.25.12: Then sweet-spoken Saramā, touching her, spoke to Sītā, who was speaking thus, words choked with tears.
t.6.25.13: If this is your wish, then I shall go, Jānakī; having grasped the enemy's intention, see me return to you.
t.6.25.15: Having heard the resolve of that evil-minded one, she, who discerned his intent, then quickly went back once more to the Aśoka grove.
t.6.25.14: Having spoken thus, she then went near that rākṣasa and heard what was being said by Rāvaṇa together with his ministers.
t.6.25.17: When Saramā, sweet of speech, had come back, Sītā embraced her very affectionately and herself offered her a seat.
t.6.25.16: Having entered there once more, she saw the daughter of Janaka waiting for her, like Śrī herself, whose lotus has slipped away.
t.6.25.18: Sitting here at ease, tell me everything truly: what is the resolve of that cruel, evil-minded Rāvaṇa?
t.6.25.19: Thus addressed by the trembling Sītā, Saramā recounted everything that had been said by Rāvaṇa together with his minister.
t.6.25.21: Let Maithilī be given back to the lord of men, having first been duly honoured. What wondrous thing happened in Janasthāna is sufficient as an example for you.
t.6.25.20: O Vaidehī, the lord of the Rākṣasas was indeed earnestly urged by his mother, and also by the aged minister Aviddha, to set you free.
t.6.25.23: Though he has been addressed at length in this way by his elder ministers and by his mother, he cannot bring himself to release you, just as one devoted to wealth cannot let go of his wealth.
t.6.25.22: The leaping across the ocean, the sight of Hanumān, and the slaying of rākṣasas in battle: what mere human on earth could accomplish these?
t.6.25.24: O Maithilī, as long as he is not slain in battle he cannot bring himself to release you. Such indeed is the firm resolve of that cruel one and his ministers.
t.6.25.26: Having slain Rāvaṇa in battle with sharpened arrows, Rāma will surely lead you back to Ayodhyā, O dark-eyed one.
t.6.25.27: Meanwhile a sound mingled with kettledrums and conches was heard, the sound of all the armies, making the surface of the earth tremble.
t.6.25.25: Thus this firm resolve has taken hold of him, arising from a greed that courts death: out of fear he is unable to release you unless he is overthrown in battle, for it will come only through the slaughter of all the rākṣasas and of himself.
t.6.25.28: But on hearing that clamour of the monkey army, the servants of the king of the Rākṣasas dwelling in Laṅkā, their vigour lost and their bearing overcome by dejection, see no good ahead because of the faults of their king.
